metadata.title: 2002 Case 09
metadata.original_presentation: An 80-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital because of sudden unilateral blindness.

required.content: What is the patient's medical history?
required.response: The patient had a long history of medical problems including hypertension, mitral and tricuspid regurgitation treated by valvuloplasties, atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin, right-sided congestive heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, chronic renal insufficiency with a baseline creatinine level of 2.4 mg/dL, and chronic pancytopenia due to congestive splenomegaly with hypersplenism. She had a left carotid endarterectomy one year before admission.

teaching_points.content: A comprehensive medical history is crucial in understanding the patient's current condition and potential complications.

required.content: What recent surgeries has the patient undergone?
required.response: Twenty-two days before admission, the patient underwent an elective open cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis and a splenectomy due to increasing blood transfusion requirements and anemia.

teaching_points.content: Recent surgeries can have significant implications on a patient's current health status and may contribute to new symptoms.

required.content: What were the patient's symptoms prior to admission?
required.response: Six days before admission, the patient experienced a headache with severe pain in the left eye, which worsened. Examination showed preseptal cellulitis of the left eye with extension across the nasal bridge.

teaching_points.content: Preseptal cellulitis can lead to serious complications if not treated promptly, including vision loss.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)
refuting_evidence: none directly refuting

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis)
supporting_evidence: headache with severe pain in the left eye
refuting_evidence: no mention of jaw claudication or scalp tenderness

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Ischemic Optic Neuropathy
supporting_evidence: history of hypertension and vascular disease
refuting_evidence: no specific refuting evidence

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Orbital Cellulitis
supporting_evidence: headache with severe pain in the left eye
preseptal cellulitis of the left eye
refuting_evidence: sudden blindness is less typical without more severe infection signs
additional_information_needed: CT or MRI of the orbit

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Retinal Detachment
refuting_evidence: no mention of flashes or floaters
recent preseptal cellulitis

required.content: What were the findings on physical examination upon admission?
required.response: The patient was cachectic with a temperature of 37.2°C, pulse of 90, respirations of 20, and blood pressure of 170/75 mm Hg. There was complete loss of light perception in the left eye, occlusion of the central retinal artery, swelling of the optic disk, severely decreased motility in all directions, and complete ptosis. The right eye had visual acuity of 20/400. The heart was enlarged with an irregular rhythm and a grade 2 holosystolic murmur. The lungs were clear.

teaching_points.content: A thorough physical examination can provide critical clues to the underlying diagnosis, especially in complex cases.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)
key_features: occlusion of the central retinal artery
supporting_evidence: occlusion of the central retinal artery
additional_information_needed: Ophthalmologic examination to confirm retinal findings

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis)
refuting_evidence: No mention of jaw claudication
No elevated ESR reported

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Orbital Cellulitis
supporting_evidence: headache with severe pain in the left eye
preseptal cellulitis of the left eye
refuting_evidence: No fever
No proptosis reported
additional_information_needed: CT or MRI of the orbit

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Ischemic Optic Neuropathy
supporting_evidence: history of hypertension and vascular disease
refuting_evidence: No specific mention of altitudinal field defect

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Endophthalmitis
refuting_evidence: No mention of red eye or hypopyon
No fever

required.content: What imaging studies were performed and what were the findings?
required.response: A cranial MRI showed thickening of the mucosa of the left maxillary, sphenoid, and ethmoid sinuses, a retention cyst in the right sphenoid sinus, and smooth, mild dural enhancement. There was enhancement of preseptal and nasal soft-tissue swelling. The superior ophthalmic veins appeared normal with no evidence of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

teaching_points.content: Imaging studies are essential in diagnosing and assessing the extent of disease, particularly in cases involving potential orbital or sinus involvement.

required.content: What laboratory tests were performed and what were the results?
required.response: Laboratory tests included blood cultures, which were sterile, and tests for antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor, which were negative. A lumbar puncture was performed, and further laboratory tests were conducted.

teaching_points.content: Laboratory tests can help rule out infectious and autoimmune causes in complex clinical presentations.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis)
supporting_evidence: headache with severe pain in the left eye
refuting_evidence: no mention of elevated ESR or CRP
no jaw claudication or scalp tenderness reported

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
supporting_evidence: occlusion of the central retinal artery
history of atrial fibrillation and peripheral vascular disease
refuting_evidence: presence of preseptal cellulitis and sinusitis may suggest an alternative cause

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Orbital Cellulitis
supporting_evidence: preseptal cellulitis of the left eye
headache with severe pain in the left eye
refuting_evidence: no fever or systemic signs of infection
blood cultures were sterile
additional_information_needed: further imaging to assess for abscess or deeper infection

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Ischemic Optic Neuropathy
supporting_evidence: history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation
refuting_evidence: presence of preseptal cellulitis and sinusitis may suggest an alternative cause

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Mucormycosis
supporting_evidence: thickening of the mucosa of the sinuses
refuting_evidence: no evidence of cavernous sinus thrombosis
no mention of immunocompromised state

required.content: What treatments were administered during the hospital stay?
required.response: The patient was treated with nafcillin, ceftriaxone, metronidazole, furosemide, lisinopril, spironolactone, hydrochlorothiazide, ranitidine, digoxin, heparin, acetaminophen, morphine, and high-dose methylprednisolone.

teaching_points.content: Management of complex cases often involves a multidisciplinary approach and the use of multiple medications to address various aspects of the patient's condition.

final_diagnosis.name: Bilateral central retinal artery occlusion with optic nerve ischemia
